text.p: An investigation into comments by former Los Angeles detective Mark Fuhrman about evidence planting, beatings and false arrests were "unfounded" and "ludicrous," a special panel said in a report on Monday.

Fuhrman's claims, made to an aspiring screenwriter more than 10 years ago, became a focal point of O.J. Simpson's criminal trial, in which he was acquitted of murdering his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman.

In audiotape recordings made by Laura Hart McKinney for a proposed movie, portions of which were played at Simpson's 1995 criminal trial, Fuhrman, a key prosecution witness, claimed he had falsely arrested suspects, particularly blacks, beaten suspects and either fabricated or tampered with evidence over a number of years.

But the investigation panel, made up of senior members of the Los Angeles Police Department's Internal Affairs Division and the city's Police Commission, found that the detective had lied about the events he described to McKinney.

In his book, "Murder in Brentwood," published by Regnery Publishing, Fuhrman himself acknowledged he had made up the "recollections" to McKinney. "Agreeing that we needed hard-hitting action and tough characters, I let my imagination run wild. Throughout the interviews (with McKinney) I was creating fictional situations, sometimes based loosely on true incidents," he wrote.

The would-be screenwriter's tapes were discovered by Simpson's criminal defence team and used to prove Fuhrman lied on the witness stand when he told the jury he had never used the word "nigger" in the previous 10 years. The tapes made by McKinney were peppered with the racial epithet.
The former detective, who retired from the department after the trial, subsequently pleaded no contest to a single charge of perjury and was fined and placed on probation.

Fuhrman testified at the trial that he discovered a bloody glove on Simpson's estate on the morning after the June 1994 murders which matched a blood-smeared glove found at the murder scene outside Simpson's ex-wife's home.

At a news conference to announce the panel's findings, outgoing Los Angeles Police Chief Willie Williams said there was no evidence of "systemic misconduct" by Los Angeles police officers as described by Fuhrman, but acknowledged that problem areas did exist, in particular sexual harassment by male officers against female colleagues.

Fuhrman's claim that a group called "Men Against Women" had existed at the West Los Angeles station where he worked was substantiated, Williams said, although there was no evidence that the group still existed.

In addition, the report called for increased command accountability for misconduct, expanding the disciplinary process, better deployment of female sergeants and raising expectations for the integrity of police officers.

Simpson was acquitted of the murders in October 1995 but was subsequently found liable for the deaths of Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman earlier this year in a civil wrongful death lawsuit. The jury awarded $33.5 million in damages to the families of the victims.
